questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
There are several aspects that were crucial to my decision to choose Hong Kong and HKU as my study destination. First and foremost, I have always been attracted to the cultural diversity and vibrancy of Hong Kong. I know many people who either travelled to Hong Kong or lived and worked there. I've only ever heard great things which is one reason why I've wanted to visit Hong Kong for years. As a major international city, Hong Kong offers a unique blend of Western and Eastern cultures where most of the population speaks English. I was excited to immerse myself in this dynamic and vibrant environment and learn more about different cultures and perspectives.

Another important factor for me personally was that HKU seemed to have a great supportive and inclusive community at HKU and offered a range of resources and services to help students thrive academically, socially, and personally. Furthermore I really appreciated that all classes (except some Chinese language classes) are taught in English and that the prime medium of communication at HKU is English. 

Finally, in a city such as Hong Kong where so many different cultures exists side by side and with a lot of people working in different time zones or work schedules, the city never really sleeps and one can always get ones favourite food at almost any time of day! Shout out to dim sum restaurants that open at 4am!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Though I loved my stay in Hong Kong and the city itself, I did have a few issues with the (local) residence hall I was assigned and personally I prefer the teaching style at University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy! Whenever some information were not to be found or were unclear, the department CEDARS at HKU would respond to emails really quickly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Personally I don't think I got any assistance when I arrived in HK, but I don't feel like it would really be needed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: HKU hosted a lost of diffrent kinds of orientation at arrival, which was really nice! I didn't need any assistance, but I know some people who did, and it worked really well according to them.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
There were many different on-campus housing options available. I lived in a local hall, then there is colleges (some with meal plans, some with single rooms some with double) and shared student flats. I think there were some other options, but I'm not really sure what those are called... In general most places close to the main campus is shared rooms.

I also know that CEDARS at HKU helped people who were not offered a housing spot finding a place to stay. Most people in this situation however, lived in a hostel for the first couple of weeks until finding a room. 

Furthermore, actually (if I remember correctly) only one hall is actually on campus, the rest is semi close by and some further away which I really liked!

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
As mentioned, a couple of places has meal plans. This is not very common though, so most halls, colleges, shared flats etc. has a pantry/kitchen. 

I was very unlucky and ended up living on a floor where the pantry was very close to useless (as no one ever cleaned and everything was moldy...). However, there is always boiling water and cold drinking water available in all on campus housing. 

Ps: don't let this affect your decision! I was quite moody in the beginning of my stay because of this, but I honestly didn't spend much time in the hall, met some really nice people there and ate out most of the time either ways! You can get cheap meals either at campus or all over the city and the portions are often generous (which means you can bring the leftovers with you home!).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Be aware of the conditions of the local halls. Also, contrary to what most people expect, living in a local hall actually means that international students and exchange students are rarely (if at all) included in any hall activities and most people I knew living in local halls didn't talk to any of the locals living there... as we were really excluded and they mostly didn't talk to us:((.  

The colleges has a way better environment! In hindsight I would have preferred living in the Jockey Club Student Village III, but I made a lot of international friends from the hall I lived in and ended up knowing a lot of people living in different types of housing – an experience I don't think I would be without now!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Most people was offered housing, which is incredible in HK! The housing prices in HK is really high, so just having a place to stay is brilliant! Though the quality of the housing varies I still find it incredible that most exchange students are offered on campus housing. 

My specific hall was admitted really bad, however having the prices of renting privately in HK in mind, I still think I would prefer to live in a hall. This way you will no matter what meet some other university and fellow exchange students!

A lot of the friends I made during my stay was with people living in my hall or through those people.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had no problems at all, everything is super easy and straight forward.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
To be honest I don't really recall the registration process at your HKU, but that might be because of how easy I found it.

I think you had to sign up for classes two weeks before the semester start or something like that. There was also a add-drop period for the first week (I think... we were affected by very bad weather aka typhoons and black rain which meant we had a two week add-drop period).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: One can always email CEDARS and they will answer quickly! Be aware of the 6/7 hour time difference to DK though.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful in registering for all the classes I wanted. Except one, but it turned out something went wrong with the system at the course weren't available for exchange students. However most courses I wanted were available to everyone, but it might differ from faculty to faculty (I was at the Faculty of Engineering).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't decide on all classes in advance! Go and use the one to two week add-drop period to figure out which courses you like (and where it might be easiest to make friends).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned earlier, I much prefer the teaching style at UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
In my opinion, the levels of the courses I took varied a lot. I had some very easy courses that took almost no work and then I had courses where no one seemed to know what was going on.

As I study data/computer science I heavily depend on having exercise classes, which was not really a thing at HKU. Typically each course has one to two lectures (each between one and three hours) and then one to two hour tutorials (which is typically used a phd student lecturing) a week. 

Some courses had a lot of courses work and some had almost none.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: See above answer.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
CHIN 9511 - Cantonese as a foreign language
COMP 3220 - Principles of operating systems
COMP 3258 - Functional programming
COMP 3314 - Machine learning
LING 2067 - Natural language processing

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
CHIN 9511 - Cantonese as a foreign language! If one has the opportunity to take classes outside the scope of ones bachelor/master I think Cantonese as a foreign language is a good option. It was quite demanding, as a lot of people spoke a little Canto, even though the course were supposed to be for absolute beginners. As a result of this our teacher expected everyone to be at that level. 

I also really enjoyed the machine learning class! The professor were really brilliant and the same can be said for the NLP course. Though the NLP course is mainly a lingustics course, I found it quite interesting to get another perspective, as I will likely take a "real" NLP course at UCPH.

Functional programming was fun and I learned a lot, but the course was way too difficult and most people struggled to get through. Principles of operating systems was wayyy too much work. We had one to two assignments each week and the lectures where not very interesting...

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I don't remember any unexpected costs. 

Also, personal spending does not include traveling, but rather snacks, coffee, HK milk tea, cinema, karaoke, etc.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Hong Kong is a very expensive city especially if you want western products and want to eat at western restaurants and stuff. Often, things like coffee will actually be a bit more expensive than Copenhagen (and dairy products are very expensive - 250 kilogram butter was 62HKD!) but I still think eating out is generally cheaper than Denmark. Going out is also bit expensive even though alcohol bought directly in stores is cheaper than in DK... a lot of time people just meet up outside at a pier, hangout there and buys drinks from 7-eleven.

Vegetable in supermarkets is less cheap that I expected so go to the wet markets to buy vegetables. And be aware that some instant noodles can be pricy as well!

In general in Hong Kong, you can live really cheaply but you can also choose to spend a lot of money. It totally depends on your budget and preferences.  Remember that most of the people you'll likely meet will be students who don't receive SU or has a job, so their spending will typically match that of a fairly poor student.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I only really participated in one non-academic opportunity which I really liked which was part of an Inter-Island Film festival. I'm really quite sad I didn't join the dragon boat club as that looked like amazing fun and good exercise! I also know there were plenty of hiking clubs, arts clubs (I went to one "meeting" with the calligraphy club but never really had time to go again...:(), dance clubs, culture/language clubs, sports clubs etc...

My friends at one of the colleges in Kennedy Town (student village ||| aka the place to be) also held some cultural festival activities I participated in a couple of times.

My advice is to do sign up for as many clubs as possible in the beginning and then later chose which you want to keep going to! You often have to pay a small amount in the beginning, but I think it's worth it!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Everything you can imagine! 

The cultural festival activities-things my friends did was something they just started this year and some were exchange students, so don't worry about not finding a club or other activities to join!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Dragon boat!
Smaller activities hosted by the uni (can typically be found in their daily information letter).
Join college/hall activities if possible!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go eat! Take the star ferry, and the ferries to out lying islands and go on some hikes! Visit the markets like Wan Chai Market (day market - you can find many great things there actually) and Ladies Market (night market - quite touristy). Also go jam2 caa4 (yum cha - directly translated means to drink tea but it means to go eat dim sum). You should definitely try the small local places like Sun Hing in Kennedy Town but also the really large more modern style dim sum restaurants like Victoria Harbour Restaurants. Remember dim sum is meant to share, so bring lots of friends! 

There really is something to do for every mood, person and preferences! 
Don't forget to just walk around and soak in the city (and it's sounds and smells) even though it's really hot and humid...

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
I found it easy. My uncle lived in HK for quite a while when I was younger, so HK was quite what I expected. Some people might think that the culture is a bit rude and the manners at especially local restaurants can seem bad and gross to foreigners I think, but people are always really friendly and helpful<3 

The tempo is a bit faster in Denmark, especially at the cashier's or at restaurants (it's not uncommon to queue for 30 mins before entering a bar/restaurant). 

The biggest culture shock for me was probably the heat and humidity combined... I know some people whos clothing got mouldy because of the humidity. And the amount of people almost everywhere!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Hong Kong is in a lot of ways very westerns and a lot of local and international students are very used to foreigners so it's easy socialising with everyone. As everyone needs to speak English (as the medium of instruction is always English, except language courses ofc, it's easy to communicate with everyone. I also meet a lot of local students whos ethnicity was not HK or Chinese but everyone seems really well included!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The hall culture in the local hall were the most challenging for me I think, but it's really not something that you can't get over.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
It's difficult to put into words, as I loved everything about Hong Kong! I actually liked HK so much I think I will (if in any way possible) move there at some point! Though maybe not forever... rip HK:(( 

Obviously, one of the things that makes Hong Kong so easy to be in and so enjoyeble is the perfect mixture between the east and the west - there will simply always be something for everyones taste!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Apply for the colleges in Kennedy Town! 
Prepare for really hot and humid weather.
Just enjoy Hong Kong as much as possible!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to call HK my home and making friends and acquaintances in this new place and culture completely different, and yet not, from Copenhagen. Keeping in contact with the friends I made after leaving is also really rewarding to me.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The hall... to be fair, I could have applied to change halls, but I didn't realise because it was in the second week. 

And again, it was an experience I don't think I wouldn't be without today!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go to Hong Kong!!!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
